en.title: Subjects and timetables
en.summary: School subjects, a weekly timetable and how to compare what you like.

paragraphs: Talking about school is a good way to practise the names of subjects, the time words of a timetable and the language of likes and dislikes.
Two pupils compare their timetables at a school in Glasgow.

lines.speaker: Amir
lines.text: What lessons do you have on Monday?

lines.speaker: Zoe
lines.text: Maths at nine, then English and history. After lunch we have science.

lines.speaker: Amir
lines.text: I like science, but I don't like history.

lines.speaker: Amir
lines.text: There are too many dates to learn, and the teacher gives a lot of homework.

lines.speaker: Zoe
lines.text: I prefer history to maths. What is your favourite subject?

lines.speaker: Amir
lines.text: Physical education. We play football on Wednesday afternoons.

lines.speaker: Zoe
lines.text: That is when we have art. I'm not very good at drawing.

paragraphs: **1. School subjects are uncountable names.** They do not take a plural s: maths, physics, history, English. They take a singular verb. See Introduction to Grammar: Substantives (nouns).

blocks.html:
SubjectExample
mathsMaths is difficult.
physicsPhysics is interesting.
historyHistory is my favourite.
PEPE is on Wednesday.

paragraphs: **2. Too many and too much.** Use too many with countable nouns and too much with uncountable nouns. Also learn good at, bad at and interested in. See Introduction to Grammar: Articles and determiners.

blocks.html:
PhraseExample
too manytoo many dates to learn
too muchtoo much homework
good atI'm good at maths.
bad atI'm bad at drawing.

items: A lesson lasts about an hour; a term lasts several weeks.
Americans say math, British say maths.
Break is a short rest; lunch is a longer one.

paragraphs: Pupils in Britain wear school uniform and the school year runs from September to July. In the United States the school year begins in August or September, and pupils often move from room to room for their lessons.
